stem: A team exposes a customer-support agent that can read tickets, draft replies, issue refunds, and delete user accounts. Support staff only ever need to read tickets and draft replies. Applying least-privilege principles, which change best reduces risk?

options.text: Add logging to the refund and delete tools so misuse can be audited later.
options.why: Logging is a detective control: it records misuse after it has happened rather than removing the unnecessary privilege that makes misuse possible.

options.text: Remove the refund and delete tools from the agent's configuration entirely.
options.why: Least privilege means removing capabilities the role does not require, eliminating the attack surface rather than monitoring or guarding it.

options.text: Keep all tools but add a confirmation prompt before refunds and deletions.
options.why: A confirmation is a compensating control that still leaves the dangerous capability in place; it reduces, but does not remove, the risk of a harmful action.

options.text: Replace the agent with a larger model that follows instructions more reliably.
options.why: Model size is unrelated to authorization scope; a more capable model still holds tools the role never needs.

explanation: Least privilege means removing capabilities the role does not require, eliminating the attack surface rather than monitoring or guarding it. Logging and confirmations are detective or compensating controls, not removal of unnecessary privilege, and model size is unrelated to authorization scope.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide v1.0, section 8; Claude docs — Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections

stem: An application sends the same 8,000-token system prompt and policy document on every request, followed by a short, varying user message. Latency and cost are both concerns. Which optimization most directly addresses both?

options.text: Truncate the policy document to the first 1,000 tokens.
options.why: Truncation loses policy content the application needs; it trades correctness for savings instead of reusing the stable prefix.

options.text: Switch to the smallest available model regardless of task fit.
options.why: Downsizing the model blindly risks output quality and does nothing about resending 8,000 static tokens on every request.

options.text: Place the static system prompt and policy before the dynamic content and enable prompt caching.
options.why: Ordering stable content first and enabling prompt caching lets the repeated prefix be reused, reducing both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without discarding required context.

options.text: Move the policy document into a few-shot example block.
options.why: Relocating the policy into examples does not create a cacheable, reusable prefix; the same tokens are still processed on every request.

explanation: Ordering stable content first and enabling prompt caching lets repeated prefixes be reused, reducing both time-to-first-token and per-request cost without discarding required context. Truncation loses needed policy, downsizing blindly risks quality, and relocating content to few-shot examples does not create a cacheable prefix.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide v1.0, section 8; Claude docs — Prompt caching

stem: A RAG system suddenly returns confident but incorrect answers after a document refresh, while latency and model version are unchanged. What is the most likely first place to investigate?

options.text: The model weights have silently changed.
options.why: The model version is stated to be unchanged, and nothing about a document refresh would alter model weights.

options.text: The retrieval/indexing step is returning irrelevant or stale chunks.
options.why: Confident-but-wrong answers following a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point to retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings.

options.text: The temperature setting is too low.
options.why: Temperature affects randomness of generation; it would not be triggered by a document refresh and does not explain a sudden shift to wrong answers.
The context window is a property of the model version, which is unchanged; a document refresh cannot shrink it.

explanation: Confident-but-wrong answers following a document refresh, with model and latency unchanged, point to retrieval feeding the model poor context, for example a broken re-index or mismatched embeddings. The other options would not be triggered specifically by a document refresh.
reference: CCAR-P Exam Guide v1.0, section 8; Claude docs — Reduce hallucinations
